notes.meaning: The Lord spoke to Moses with direct instructions to begin the ordination of the priests. The book of Leviticus shifts here from giving sacrificial laws to telling the story of appointing the men who would offer those sacrifices. God Himself chose the priests, showing that religious leaders cannot appoint themselves.

God told Moses to gather Aaron, his sons, their priestly garments, the holy oil, and the required sacrificial animals at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. The entire assembly of community leaders was called together to watch. Having the people witness the ceremony proved that God, not family favoritism, had placed Aaron and his sons into office.

Moses obeyed God completely and gathered the leaders of Israel at the entrance of the sacred tent. He announced to the crowd that what they were about to see was commanded by the Lord. This showed the nation that their worship system rested entirely on God's authority.

Moses brought Aaron and his sons forward and washed their entire bodies with water. This complete bathing showed that anyone serving God must first be cleansed from the defilement of sin. Priests could not enter God's presence without this outward sign of an inward spiritual washing.

Moses dressed Aaron in the high priest's sacred garments, including the woven tunic, the sash, the robe, and the ephod vest. He placed the chestpiece on him, which held the Urim and Thummim, sacred lots used to learn God's decisions. Finally, he placed the turban on Aaron's head with a gold plate engraved 'Holy to the Lord,' marking Aaron as the people's dedicated mediator before God.

Moses took the scented anointing oil and anointed the tabernacle and everything inside it, consecrating them, which means setting them apart as holy for God. He sprinkled oil on the bronze altar of sacrifice seven times and anointed its tools and the washing basin. Sprinkling the altar seven times marked it as completely dedicated to making future offerings holy.

Moses poured the holy anointing oil generously over Aaron's head to consecrate him as high priest. Other items were merely sprinkled, but the oil was poured richly on Aaron until it ran down his beard. This generous pouring pointed ahead to the Holy Spirit being poured without measure upon Jesus Christ.

Moses brought Aaron's four sons forward and clothed them in linen tunics, sashes, and headbands, just as the Lord commanded. Their vestments were simpler than the high priest's ornate robes, but were made of clean white linen. These garments showed that every priest was called to walk in purity and righteousness before God.

Moses brought forward the bull for the sin offering, an animal sacrificed to remove sin's guilt. Aaron and his sons pressed their hands firmly on the bull's head. By laying their hands on the animal, they acknowledged their own sins and transferred their guilt to the innocent victim.

Moses slaughtered the bull and used his finger to apply its blood to the four corner horns of the altar to purify it. He poured the rest of the blood out at the base of the altar to consecrate it so it could be used for atonement, which means making peace with God through sacrifice. Moses performed these priestly actions because the Aaronic priests were not yet fully ordained.

Moses burned the best internal fat, the lobe of the liver, and the kidneys on the altar as God's portion. The rest of the bull, including its hide, meat, and dung, was carried outside the camp and burned completely to ashes. Because this sin offering was for the priests themselves, they were not allowed to eat any part of it.

Moses presented the first ram for a burnt offering, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on its head. Moses slaughtered the ram and splashed its blood against all sides of the altar. This offering declared that the priests were now devoting their entire lives to God's service.

Moses cut the ram into pieces and washed its legs and entrails with clean water. He then burned the entire animal on the altar as a pleasing aroma, an offering made by fire to the Lord. Consuming the whole ram on the altar symbolized total surrender and complete dedication to God.

Moses brought the second ram, called the ram of ordination, and the priests laid their hands on its head. After slaughtering it, Moses smeared some of its blood on the right earlobe, right thumb, and right big toe of Aaron and his sons, before sprinkling the rest on the altar. Touching these parts showed that the priests' whole persons were dedicated to God: their ears to hear His word, their hands to do His work, and their feet to walk in His ways.

Moses took the choice fat portions, the right thigh, and three kinds of unleavened bread from the basket before the Lord. He placed all these sacred items into the hands of Aaron and his sons and had them wave them before the Lord as a wave offering. Placing these sacrificial foods directly into their hands was the formal act of installing them into their priestly duties.

Moses took the waved offerings back from their hands and burned them on the altar on top of the burnt offering. He then took the ram's breast and waved it before the Lord as his own portion. Because Moses acted as the officiating priest for this installation ceremony, God gave him the priest's normal food portion.

Moses took anointing oil and sacrificial blood from the altar and sprinkled them together onto Aaron, his sons, and their garments. This double sprinkling formally consecrated both the men and the official clothes they wore. The blood provided cleansing from sin, while the holy oil symbolized the empowering presence of the Holy Spirit.

Moses directed Aaron and his sons to boil the remaining ram meat at the entrance to the sacred tent and eat it there with the holy bread. Any meat or bread left over until the next morning had to be burned with fire so it would not spoil or be treated as ordinary food. This sacred meal was a fellowship feast celebrating peace and communion between God and His newly consecrated priests.

Aaron and his sons were ordered to stay inside the courtyard at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting day and night for seven full days. Each day these ordination sacrifices were repeated to make atonement for them until their consecration was complete. Remaining separated in God's presence impressed upon them the supreme holiness of God and protected them from dying for disobedience.

Aaron and his sons did everything the Lord had commanded through Moses without changing a single detail. Their faithful obedience finished their ordination and prepared them to lead the nation in worship. True service to God always begins with humble and exact obedience to His word.
